patient_response: Ever since the divorce and moving into my own place, I keep forgetting basic things like paying bills and showing up for appointments, even when I write them down. It's gotten to the point where it's really starting to affect my day-to-day life, and I'm getting pretty worried about it.

No, I wouldn't say I feel sad, hopeless, or like I've lost interest in things I enjoy. I'm just feeling incredibly stressed, overwhelmed, and frustrated by how much I'm forgetting and how hard it is to keep up with all the new responsibilities. My overall mood is okay, but managing all of this on my own is just wearing me down.

Things really got worse about a year ago after my divorce, when I moved and took on a lead maintenance role with much more complex tasks. Since then, I've really struggled to concentrate; my mind constantly drifts off when people explain repairs to me, and I have to re-read work orders and safety memos several times just to get the information to stick.

To be honest, I'm not really sure because I haven't had much of a break from stress lately to compare. But even with simple, everyday tasks at home like paying bills or finding my keys, I still find myself struggling and spacing out just as much.

I can't really think of any times where my memory or concentration has felt completely normal lately. These struggles feel pretty constant and are really hard to shake off, even when I am trying my absolute best. It just feels like it is always happening, no matter what I'm doing.

The stress of the divorce and my new responsibilities over the last 11 months has definitely made things much worse. But looking back, I realize this isn't entirely new—even in elementary school, my teachers wrote that I was always spacing out, losing worksheets, and forgetting my homework. I think my brain has always worked this way, but with all the new demands, I just can't manage to compensate for it anymore.

I'm completely awake and aware of my surroundings, but my mind just drifts away from what's right in front of me. For instance, I'll look directly at someone at work and nod, but their words don't actually register in my head. Other times, I'll read all the way to the bottom of a work order only to realize I didn't absorb a single thing and have to start over.
No, I've never really struggled with restlessness, fidgeting, or staying seated. My issues are much more about my focus, attention, and memory rather than any kind of physical hyperactivity.

No, I don't really struggle with interrupting others or blurting things out in conversations. My issues are much more about spacing out, losing track of my things, and forgetting what I'm supposed to be doing.

No, I've never been officially diagnosed or treated for ADHD before, and this is my first time seeking an evaluation. But looking back, my elementary school teachers always wrote on my report cards that I was smart but constantly spaced out, lost my worksheets, and forgot to hand in homework I'd already finished.

In childhood, my spacing out and losing homework were mostly confined to school, and I managed to get by. But after my divorce a year ago, moving into my own place and taking on a lead maintenance role created a level of logistical pressure I'd never faced before. Managing all of my own household, finances, and a demanding job alone made my forgetfulness and half-finished tasks much worse and harder to handle over the last 11 months.

I’m stuck in this loop of double- and triple-checking my work for hours, and I can’t move on even when I know it’s already done right. It’s incredibly exhausting, and I feel like I've completely lost control of my time.

If I try to stop or get interrupted, it triggers this intense, crushing anxiety, and I feel a desperate need to restart the entire sequence from the beginning. My brain immediately floods with catastrophic "what if" thoughts, making me feel like a terrible disaster will happen and it will be entirely my fault if I don't get it "just right." I just can't quiet that loop in my head until I finish the ritual.

It’s definitely about preventing harm or a catastrophe, rather than symmetry or exactness. I get these vivid flashes of a server getting hacked because of a missed setting, or my nephew getting hurt because I didn't check a door lock. It's driven by this terrifying fear that something awful will happen and it will be entirely my fault.

They are definitely tied to plausible, real-world consequences rather than anything magical or supernatural. I obsess over actual risks, like a client's server getting hacked because of a missed configuration or my nephew getting hurt because I left a door unlocked. Even though these are real-world scenarios, the intense anxiety makes the danger feel disproportionately likely and completely catastrophic if I don't check.

Yes, the anxiety is absolutely paralyzing if I can't check, to the point where I can't focus on anything else. Because of that constant dread, I've ended up avoiding social events, family gatherings, and even hobbies like salsa dancing altogether.

Honestly, it has completely taken over my life to a severe degree. I’ve had to give up things I used to love like salsa dancing and tech meetups, and I even missed a critical family celebration because I couldn't stop checking. My productivity at work has also plummeted because I burn hours re-reviewing tasks instead of moving projects forward.

No, I don't really experience that kind of generalized worry about everyday things like my finances or relationships. My anxiety is very specifically focused on my checking rituals and the constant, terrifying fear that I'm going to make a catastrophic mistake.

I feel like I’m constantly trying to make up for eating too much, and it’s taking over how I plan my days. My primary care doctor actually suggested I come in for a psychiatric evaluation after I talked to him about how much I've been struggling with this lately.

Yes, I actually do both, and it's honestly exhausting and embarrassing to admit. Some nights after overeating, I'll force myself to throw up because I just can't stand the thought of all that food turning into weight. Other days, I try to punish myself by skipping breakfast and lunch, and forcing myself to run extra laps after soccer practice even when I'm wiped out from a 10-hour shift at the shop.

For the last few months, it's been a weekly cycle where I do this about once or twice a week. On some of those nights, I'll end up making myself throw up, while other times I try to "cancel it out" by skipping breakfast and lunch and forcing myself to run extra laps.

Yes, I absolutely freak out about gaining weight, and it's what drives all of this. I constantly check the scale at the shop and panic if I'm even a pound heavier, worrying that every slice of pizza is going straight to my gut. That fear is exactly why I'll skip meals, run until I'm exhausted, or make myself throw up just to stop the food from turning into weight.

Yes, I really struggle with that. When I look in the mirror, I don't see a guy who passed his certs and keeps trucks running; I just see a soft belly and love handles. It makes me feel like a complete failure, especially compared to the younger techs at the shop who are always posting their gym pics.

I'm not entirely sure how to break it down that way, to be honest. But those feelings of panic about my weight and feeling like a failure when I look in the mirror seem to be there constantly lately, rather than just right after a heavy night of eating.
Actually, I'm a guy, so I don't have a menstrual cycle. But the physical strain of everything else has definitely been wearing me down in other ways.

It's definitely taken a massive toll on my life. I've been turning down weekend hikes and playing worse at soccer because I'm either completely exhausted from skipping meals or sore from pushing myself too hard. Even at work, I find myself constantly distracted by planning how to "fix" what I ate instead of focusing on the trucks.
No, I don't really have concerns about other specific features of my appearance like that. My worries are pretty much entirely focused on my weight, my belly, and my overall body shape.

Well, doctor, I've started eating big amounts by myself at night because I'm embarrassed for anyone to see how much I'm eating. It's been really hard to admit, but it has gotten to a point where I knew I needed to talk to someone about it.
No, doctor, I don't do any of those things. I've never tried to make myself throw up, take laxatives, or do any kind of heavy exercising after I eat like that.

This has been happening at least once or twice a week for about five months now. Once I start eating, it feels like a switch flips and I go on autopilot, shoveling food in even while I'm telling myself to stop. I just don't feel like I have any control over it.

Yes, I do both of those things. I eat so fast that I barely even taste the food, sometimes finishing a whole plate before the second quarter of the Saints game even starts. I'll also keep going until my stomach feels so tight and uncomfortable that I have to lean back in my recliner and unbutton my pants, feeling almost sick.

Before I start, I feel incredibly lonely and empty because the house is so quiet since my grandbaby moved away, and during it, I'm just on autopilot and not really thinking. Afterward, I feel so heavy, deeply ashamed, and guilty, calling myself weak and wondering how I let food take the place of my family.
I haven't really noticed any changes in that area, doctor. It's not something I've really thought about or paid much attention to lately.

It has really isolated me, doctor. I've started turning down church potlucks and dinner invitations because I'm so embarrassed and worried I'll overeat there or come home and binge, so I just stay home instead. It also leaves me sitting up late at night feeling incredibly heavy, ashamed, and calling myself weak for letting food run my life.

Yes, doctor, I can confirm that. It has been happening at least once or twice a week for about five months now, ever since my daughter and grandbaby moved away. It has definitely been a regular pattern for me for longer than three months.

If anyone starts talking about the accident or safety audits, I'll shut the conversation down or find an excuse to leave the room immediately.

On top of that, I’m so irritable that I snap and raise my voice at my wife or coworkers over nothing, and then I just spend the night hating myself for it.

It’s not tied to one specific threat, but more like a constant feeling that disaster is always just around the corner. No matter if I'm at work, sitting in church, or at home, I'm always watching exits, listening for odd noises, and running worst-case scenarios in my head. It makes everything, even letting my kids ride in the car with me, feel like an accident waiting to happen.

These feelings have been hanging over me pretty much continuously for well over a year now. They started just a few weeks after the accident at the plant, and it has been a non-stop struggle ever since.

My whole sense of worth feels tied up in what I weigh and how my body looks, and it’s taking over my life. It has gotten to the point where I can't seem to focus on anything else, and I just really need some help.

I actually do both. It feels like a switch flips in my brain and I just can't stop eating until I'm uncomfortably stuffed.

Yes, I do, and I feel incredibly ashamed to admit it. After those nights where I overeat at crew cookouts or after softball, I end up making myself throw up or taking extra laxatives to 'fix' it so it doesn't show on the scale. It's become a weekly cycle for me, sometimes even more often if work has been really stressful.

For the last few months, it's been a weekly cycle where I end up purging at least once a week, sometimes more if work stress is really high. I only do it right after those episodes where I've eaten way past full, specifically to 'fix' things so it doesn't show on the scale the next morning.

Yes, it’s a constant, daily struggle for me, not tied to any specific event at all. Every morning I stand in front of the mirror in my work pants and hi-vis vest, deciding if I'm a "good" or "disgusting" person based entirely on how big I look and what the scale says. It completely overrides any sense of worth from what I actually achieve at work or at home.
Typically, it's about once a week that I binge and then end up throwing up or taking laxatives. But if work has been especially stressful, it can definitely happen more than once in a week.

I'm not really sure of any exact numbers, but my weight hasn't seemed to change drastically. I work so hard to prevent it from changing, so I don't really have any specific weight fluctuation details to share.

Yes, that's accurate for the last few months. It happens at least once a week, though if work is really stressful, it can easily be more than once. It's just a constant, weekly cycle that I feel really stuck in.

Yes, both. Yes, absolutely. I constantly feel wired and jumpy, like I'm just waiting for something terrible to happen. It doesn't even matter if I'm in a safe place, like sitting on the couch with my wife or trying to watch a ball game—I just can't shake that feeling.

No, I don't really feel like I'm outside of my body or that things aren't real. It's more of an intense feeling of panic and physical tension, like my chest tightening up, rather than feeling disconnected like that.

No, I haven't experienced any gaps in my memory or periods where I couldn't recall what happened. In fact, I remember the accident and everything surrounding it all too clearly. It's like it's completely burned into my mind.

No, it has been completely constant and unshakeable since it first started nearly two years ago. I haven't had a single moment of doubt, even though my wife and bandmates keep trying to convince me I'm wrong. The patterns and evidence are just too clear for me to ignore.
